title: Mento Entrepreneurship Workshop — 4 Weeks
subtitle: From Curiosity to a 60-Second Pitch
description: A 4-week guided journey with Mento. Learn how real entrepreneurs find problems, dig deeper than complaints, test their ideas, and pitch. Ends with a hands-on simulation challenge.

lessons.title: Welcome to the Workshop

content.intro: Hi, I'm Mento. Over the next 4 weeks we'll go through 7 chapters of discovery, ideas, and action. Ready?
content.key_takeaway: The world doesn't need you to be perfect. It needs you to be CURIOUS.
content.mento_says: Hi! I'm Mento. Over 28 lessons we'll go from 'I have no ideas' to 'here's my 60-second pitch'. Each lesson is a tiny experiment — there are no wrong answers.

cards.title: Week 1
cards.body: Discover the entrepreneur inside you — and why every complaint is a hidden idea.

cards.title: Week 2
cards.body: Fall in love with the problem. Train your brain with the Five WHYs.

cards.title: Week 3
cards.body: Build, test, and pitch. Customer profile → idea scorecard → 60-second pitch.

cards.title: Week 4
cards.body: Apply everything in the Complaint Detective simulation.

content.question: What's a problem you noticed today — even a tiny one?
content.story_hook: Whitney Wolfe was 22 when she got fed up with how dating apps treated women — so she built Bumble. Today: $2B+. The problem matters more than the credentials.

lessons.coaching_moment: Curiosity is the entrepreneur's superpower. You don't need to be the smartest — just the most observant.

lessons.title: Who Is an Entrepreneur?

content.intro: An entrepreneur is someone who sees a problem the world is ignoring — and decides to do something about it.
content.question: What comes to your mind when you hear the word 'Entrepreneur'?
content.key_takeaway: Entrepreneurs aren't born with a magic gene. They notice problems, and act.
content.mento_says: Most people walk past problems every day. Entrepreneurs stop, look closer, and ask 'why hasn't anyone fixed this?'

quiz.question: Which of these describes an entrepreneur best?
options: Someone with a lot of money to invest
Someone who notices a problem and acts on it
Someone with a fancy degree from a top college
Someone born with a special gift
quiz.explanation: Money, degrees, and 'gifts' help — but the core skill is NOTICING + ACTING. That's it.

lessons.coaching_moment: Notice the word 'NOTICE' — entrepreneurs are first observers, then doers.

lessons.title: Types of Entrepreneurs

cards.title: The Creator
cards.body: Loves making new things. Turns ideas into products. Example: designing a cool school bag.

cards.title: The Seller
cards.body: Good at convincing people. Finds ways to reach customers. Example: selling handmade bookmarks.

cards.title: The Problem Solver
cards.body: Spots problems and fixes them. Example: a better timetable planner for students.

cards.title: The Leader
cards.body: Brings people together. Builds and manages a team.

cards.title: The Innovator
cards.body: Thinks differently. Comes up with unique ideas. Example: a smart water bottle that reminds you to drink.

content.key_takeaway: There's no single 'entrepreneur type'. Pick the one that sounds most like you.
content.intro: Entrepreneurs come in different shapes. Read each card and ask yourself: 'Does this sound like me?'

lessons.coaching_moment: There's no single 'right' type — most great founders blend two or three.

lessons.title: The BIG Myths About Entrepreneurs

content.intro: Movies and reels make entrepreneurship look like a magic gift. The truth is much simpler — and much more useful for you. Let's set the record straight, one myth at a time.

myths.myth: You need a GENIUS idea no one has ever thought of.
myths.reality: Most great companies solve OBVIOUS problems — just better, faster, or cheaper than anyone else.

myths.myth: Entrepreneurs are born — you have it or you don't.
myths.reality: Entrepreneurial thinking is a SKILL. Like cricket. Like cooking. You practise and get better.

myths.myth: You need to be RICH to start a business.
myths.reality: Most people start with almost no money. Ideas don't need bank accounts.
They feel fear every day. They just act ANYWAY — because the problem matters more than the fear.

founder_spotlight.name: Ritesh Agarwal
founder_spotlight.story: Dropped out of college at 19 with no money, just frustration about dirty hotels. Built OYO into a $9B chain operating across 35+ countries.
founder_spotlight.lesson: He didn't have a 'genius idea'. He had a clear, common problem he refused to ignore.

lessons.coaching_moment: Every myth you believe is a door that stays closed. Knock them down.

lessons.title: Every Complaint is a Clue

content.intro: Don't just listen to what people say they want. Watch what they struggle with. Every complaint is a HIDDEN BUSINESS IDEA.

examples.idea: A pre-order app for regular market customers

content.rule: RULE #1: Train your ears. Every complaint is a clue. 🎯

lessons.coaching_moment: Watch what frustrates people, not just what they say they want.

lessons.title: Worksheet: The Complaint Collector

fields.name: complaint
fields.label: Complaint I heard
fields.placeholder: e.g. 'The water tank overflows every monsoon'

fields.name: idea
fields.label: My business idea
fields.placeholder: e.g. 'Smart water-level alerts for housing societies'

lessons.coaching_moment: Talk to 5 different ages — kid, teen, parent, shopkeeper, elder. Variety = better ideas.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Hunt 5 Real Complaints
lessons.summary: Step away from the screen. Talk to 5 real humans. Bring back their case files.

content.intro: Now go out into the real world. Mento needs FIELD evidence — not just notebook ideas. Talk to 5 humans of different ages, ask them what bugs them about their day, and capture each as a case file (text, photo, or 30-sec voice note). Your case files will reappear in Week 4's Complaint Detective game — so the better your hunt, the more clues you'll have.

schema.brief: Find 5 different humans (kid, teen, parent, shopkeeper, elder works best). Ask: 'What's something that bugs you about your day?' Record what they said as a case file.

lessons.coaching_moment: The best founders are great LISTENERS. Don't argue with their complaint, don't try to solve it on the spot — just capture exactly what they said. Real problems hide in real words.

lessons.title: Mento's Three Tests: PAIN, SIZE, GAP

content.intro: Once you have an idea, you need to test it BEFORE building anything. Three quick tests separate good ideas from time-wasters. Run every idea through these three filters before you spend a single rupee.

tests.name: PAIN
tests.question: Is the problem painful enough that people will actually pay to fix it?

tests.name: SIZE
tests.question: How many people share this problem? 10? 10,000? 10 million?

tests.name: GAP
tests.question: Is anyone solving it? If yes, are they doing it badly enough that you can do it 10x better?

content.key_takeaway: PAIN × USE × WIN — if any score is low, the idea probably isn't ready yet.

lessons.coaching_moment: All three tests must pass. Ideas that fail any one of these usually fail in real life.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Apply the 3 Tests to Your Best Complaint

fields.name: pain_score
fields.label: PAIN: How much does this bother people? (1-5)

fields.name: size_colony
fields.label: SIZE: People in my colony with this problem

fields.name: size_city
fields.label: SIZE: People in my city with this problem

fields.name: why_better
fields.label: GAP: Why mine would be better

lessons.coaching_moment: If your idea fails one of the three tests, that's GOOD news — you saved months of effort.

lessons.title: Warm-up Game: Idea Lab

fields.question: Which of these is the BEST clue that you've found a real problem worth solving?

options.label: Many people complain about it again and again
It's something you saw on TV
Your friend says it's a good idea

fields.explanation: Repeated complaints from many people = a real, widespread problem. That's the PAIN test in action.

fields.explanation: GAP = is there a gap in current solutions? If everyone already has it, it's not a fresh opportunity.

fields.question: Which is a MYTH about entrepreneurs?

options.label: You need to be born a genius to be one

fields.explanation: Entrepreneurship is built skill by skill — not magic genes. Anyone curious enough can start.

fields.question: Why is 'Every complaint is a clue' a good entrepreneur mindset?

options.label: Complaints are negative and you should ignore them
Complaints reveal hidden problems people would pay to fix

fields.explanation: Behind every complaint is a problem someone would pay to solve. That's where opportunity lives.

prompts: Which of the 5 complaints you collected stuck with you the most? Why?
Which 'type' of entrepreneur are you most like — Inventor, Solver, Builder, or Connector?

weeks.title: Fall in Love With the Problem
weeks.summary: Most beginners get attached to their idea. Great entrepreneurs obsess over the problem. Learn the Five WHYs and the Idea Machine.

lessons.title: Fall in Love With the PROBLEM, Not the Solution

content.intro: Most young entrepreneurs get attached to their idea. Great entrepreneurs obsess over the problem.
content.rule: Your solution will change many times. The problem stays the same.
content.story_hook: Diya's mother loses her keys. Diya wants to invent unbreakable keys. Mento says: WAIT — let's ask WHY first.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you love your idea more than the problem, you'll defend the idea even when it's wrong. Stay loyal to the problem.

lessons.title: The Five WHYs — Mento's Digging Tool

content.intro: When someone complains, don't take it at face value. Ask 'Why?' five times — each time you get closer to the REAL problem (and therefore the real opportunity).

example_chain.answer: They fall loose in her handbag.
Her handbag has no compartment for keys.
Most bags are empty bags — no organisation.

example_chain.why: Why haven't bag makers added it?
example_chain.answer: Nobody asked them to — people just accepted the problem.
Bags are designed with ZERO thought for what working women need every day.

content.key_takeaway: Surface problem: 'lost keys'. Real problem: 'bags aren't user-friendly'. THAT'S a billion-rupee market.
content.mento_says: It feels weird to ask 'why' five times in a row. Do it anyway. The 5th why is where the gold is.

lessons.coaching_moment: Most people stop at WHY #2. The real opportunity hides at WHY #4 or #5.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Your Five WHYs
lessons.coaching_moment: If your 5th 'why' sounds like a feeling (frustration, fear, embarrassment), you've struck gold.

lessons.title: Practice the Five WHYs with a Real Customer (Voice)
lessons.coaching_moment: Real customer-interviewing is messy and your job is to dig — these AI personas resist easy answers on purpose.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Talk to 3 Real Humans This Week
lessons.summary: AI personas are great practice. Real people are where ideas survive contact with reality.

schema.brief: Pick the strongest complaint from Week 1. Find 3 different real humans who have that problem. Ask them 4 questions and write down their EXACT words (not your summary). Try not to pitch — just dig.
interview_questions: When was the LAST time this problem bothered you? Tell me the story.
What did you do about it? (If 'nothing' — why not?)
On a 1-10 scale, how painful is this? What would make it a 10?
If a perfect fix existed, what would you pay for it? (Real number — ₹0 is OK.)
persona_prompts: Someone in a different city / school / neighborhood
guardrails: Quote their actual words — not your interpretation.
If they say 'great idea!' — ask for a story instead. Compliments aren't data.

lessons.coaching_moment: If 3 real people don't have the problem strongly, you don't have a problem — you have a hobby. Better to learn this now than after 6 months of building.

lessons.title: The Idea Machine — 4 Sources of Great Ideas

content.intro: Ideas don't strike like lightning — they come from systematic observation. Train these 4 idea sources and you'll never run out.

sources.title: Your Own Frustration
sources.body: The best entrepreneurs solve problems they personally feel.

sources.title: Things People Complain About
sources.body: Listen for 'I hate it when...' or 'Why does nobody just...'

sources.title: Who Is Being Ignored?
sources.body: OYO made hotels affordable for travellers big chains ignored.

quiz.question: Which is the BEST source of business ideas?
options: Brainstorming alone in a quiet room
Watching what frustrates people in their daily lives
Asking your friends what they'd buy
quiz.explanation: Friends often say nice things to be supportive. Watching real frustration in real moments tells the truth.

lessons.coaching_moment: Ideas come from constraints, not from staring at the ceiling. Use these 4 sources daily.

lessons.title: Worksheet: The Big Brainstorm — No Wrong Answers!

schema.instruction: Set a timer for 5 minutes. Write as many ideas as possible. Don't stop — no wrong answers!

lessons.coaching_moment: Quantity → Quality. Push past the obvious 5 ideas to reach the breakthrough at #15.

lessons.title: Falguni Nayar — Started Nykaa at 50
lessons.backstory: Falguni was a top banker at Kotak Mahindra. At 50 — when most people think about retiring — she quit her job to start Nykaa, an online beauty store. She built it into India's first woman-led unicorn, taking it public in 2021.
lessons.takeaway: There is no 'too late' to start. Customer obsession beats age.

weeks.title: Build, Test, Pitch
weeks.summary: Turn your idea into something real. Build a paper prototype, define a customer, and write a 60-second pitch you can deliver out loud.

lessons.title: How Ideas Become Products

content.intro: An idea on paper is worth nothing. Real customers buy real solutions. Now it's time to think about how your idea becomes a thing people can actually use.

value_axes.title: Saves TIME
value_axes.body: Ola saves 20 mins waiting. Zomato saves the walk.

value_axes.title: Saves MONEY
value_axes.body: If your solution costs less than the alternative, people switch.

value_axes.title: Removes PAIN
value_axes.body: Genuine daily pain — 'finally someone fixed this!'

content.mento_says: Don't try to build the perfect product. Build the smallest version that solves ONE part of the problem. Ship it. Learn. Iterate.

lessons.coaching_moment: An idea is a hypothesis. A product is the test. Ship the smallest test you can.

lessons.title: What Will Customers Actually Pay For?

content.intro: Every business needs at least one person who pays for the value. Knowing exactly who that person is — name, age, daily routine — is the foundation of everything else.
examples: ₹10 cup of chai (saves time at the railway station)
₹250 cafe coffee (creates joy — and a place to sit)
₹500/month music subscription (saves the pain of buying songs)
₹2,000 noise-cancelling headphones (reduces pain of noisy hostels)
content.payer_note: The PAYER isn't always the user. A parent pays ₹500/month for a kid's tuition app. A school pays ₹50,000/year for a teacher tool. Find the person whose hand opens the wallet.

lessons.coaching_moment: If everyone is your customer, no one is your customer. Pick ONE specific person.

lessons.title: Unit Economics: Price − Cost = Margin
lessons.content:
The single rule: If one customer costs you more than they pay, selling more makes you LOSE more.

For every idea, work out three numbers:

  • Price — what one customer pays you, once.
  • Cost — what it costs you to deliver to that one customer (materials, packaging, delivery, your time).
  • Margin — Price minus Cost. The money left over.

Example: Lemonade stand. Price ₹20. Cost (lemon + sugar + cup + ice) ₹12. Margin = ₹8 per glass. To make ₹800 you need to sell 100 glasses.

Why Stayzilla died: They were charging less per booking than it cost them to support that booking. Negative margin. Every new customer = more loss. Scale didn't save them; scale killed them.

Mento's rule of thumb for school businesses: Margin should be at least 30% of price. If it's less, you're working for free.
lessons.coaching_moment: Most school business ideas die on Cost — students forget to count their own time. If a tiffin takes you an hour to make, that hour is part of cost.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Your Unit Economics

fields.name: product
fields.label: What ONE thing are you selling?

fields.name: time_minutes
fields.label: Minutes of YOUR time per unit

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Margin you calculated (Price − all costs, in ₹)

fields.name: break_even
fields.label: How many you need to sell to make ₹1,000 in profit?

lessons.coaching_moment: If your margin is under 30% of price, raise price OR cut cost OR pick a different product. Don't try to win on volume yet.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Who Is YOUR Customer?

fields.name: monthly_income
fields.label: Monthly household income (₹, choose a bracket)

lessons.coaching_moment: Specific is better than vague. 'Class 8 students who play cricket' beats 'school kids'.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Your Idea Scorecard

schema.instruction: Rate your idea 1-5 on each dimension. Be honest — this helps you improve it.

axes.name: real_problem
axes.label: The problem is REAL and painful

axes.name: excited
axes.label: I am EXCITED to work on this

market_size_axis.label: How big is this market in India?

lessons.coaching_moment: Score honestly. A 6/10 idea you ship beats a 10/10 idea that stays in your notebook.

lessons.title: Field Mission: The ₹0 Demand Test
lessons.summary: Before you build, prove someone actually wants it. Spend ₹0. Get 5 real signals.

schema.brief: You have 48 hours. Without building your product, get 5 people to do something real — pay, sign up, send a deposit, share their phone number, or commit a date. A 'like' is not data. A 'maybe' is not data. Action is data.

options.label: Make a Google Form / Tally form 'Pre-order list' and share in 1 WhatsApp group. Count real names + phone numbers.
Post a paper poster in your colony / canteen with a real WhatsApp number. Count how many DM you in 48h.
Make a 1-slide 'menu' on your phone. Show it to 10 people face-to-face. Count how many ask 'when is this available?'
Pre-sell. Ask for ₹50 deposit to reserve a spot. (Refund if you don't deliver.) Count rupees in.
Build a 1-page mockup with Canva / pencil. Show to 5 people. Ask: 'On a 1-10 scale, would you use this?' Record exact answers.

guardrails: ZERO money spent. Free tools only.
Don't build the actual product. Only test if people care.
Document with screenshots / photos / WhatsApp screen recordings.

lessons.coaching_moment: 5 strangers > 50 friends. Friends say yes to be nice. Strangers tell you the truth.

lessons.title: The 60-Second Pitch Formula

content.intro: A great pitch has 3 parts and takes 60 seconds. Master the formula and you can pitch anything — to a teacher, a parent, a teammate, or an investor.

parts.name: Who It Helps
parts.template: This helps _____ and there are about _____ people with this problem

parts.name: Why It's Different
parts.template: Unlike _____, my solution is different because _____

parts.name: The Ask
parts.template: I am looking for _____ to help me _____ so that _____

founder_spotlight.name: Tony Xu
founder_spotlight.story: Pitched investors with one slide: a photo of his mom struggling to deliver food. The whole pitch was 60 seconds.
founder_spotlight.lesson: A clear story beats a fancy deck. Make the listener FEEL the problem.

lessons.coaching_moment: Your pitch is for the listener, not for you. Cut everything they don't need.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Build Your 60-Second Pitch

fields.name: who_it_helps
fields.label: This helps _____ and there are about _____ people with this

fields.name: ask
fields.label: I'm looking for _____ to help me _____ so that _____

lessons.coaching_moment: Read your pitch out loud. If you stumble, the line is too long.

lessons.coaching_moment: Even pros feel nervous on stage. The trick: practice 10x more than you think you need.

lessons.coaching_moment: Mento will score your pitch on 5 axes and speak back specific rewrites. Try 3 times.

What is your margin per customer in rupees, and does that feel honest?

lessons.coaching_moment: Honesty here = clarity later. If the numbers are bad, that's gold — it tells you exactly what to fix.

lessons.title: Ritesh Agarwal — Started OYO at 17
lessons.backstory: At 17, Ritesh travelled across India and noticed budget hotels were unreliable: dirty rooms, no Wi-Fi, surprise prices. He started OYO to standardize them. By 21, OYO was in 100+ Indian cities. He skipped college.
lessons.takeaway: Your age is not the problem. Your observation is the asset.
lessons.reflection_prompt: What problem do you notice that adults seem to ignore?

lessons.title: Who Do You Build With? (Co-founders & Equity)
lessons.content:
Reality check: Most failed startups don't die because of bad ideas. They die because the founders stopped trusting each other.

Housing.com (Week 4 failure card) shipped beautiful tech but lost their CEO to a public Twitter meltdown over equity and control. Same product. Different co-founder chemistry. Different ending.

Mento's three filters for a co-founder:

  • Complementary, not identical. If you're the 'idea person', find a 'builder person'. Two visionaries = two egos.
  • Tested under stress. Have you worked on something hard with them for at least 3 months? Group project, hackathon, school fest? Smooth-on-coffee ≠ partner.
  • Hard conversations, easily. Can you tell them they're wrong without it becoming a fight?

Splitting equity (even with friends):

  • 50/50 is the comfortable trap. Avoid it unless you genuinely do equal work. 50/50 means no one can break a tie.
  • Vesting: Even with siblings — agree that equity unlocks over 4 years. Day 1, no one owns anything. If someone leaves in month 2, the company is safe.
  • Write it down. A 1-page agreement signed by both is worth more than a thousand 'we trust each other'.

Solo is OK too. Sridhar Vembu ran Zoho for years before adding leaders. Don't take a co-founder because it 'looks cooler'. Take one because you genuinely cannot build it without them.
lessons.coaching_moment: The hardest conversation in a startup is the first one — about money. Get it over with on day 1.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Your Co-founder Filter

fields.name: complement
fields.label: What do they bring that you DON'T have?

fields.name: stress_test
fields.label: Hardest thing you've done together. What did it teach you about them?
fields.placeholder: e.g. 'Science fair — they don't give up'

fields.name: hard_convo
fields.label: Last time you told them something uncomfortable. How did they take it?

fields.name: equity_split
fields.label: If you started today, what % would you each get and WHY?
fields.placeholder: e.g. '55/45 because I had the idea but they're doing the heavy build'

fields.name: alternative
fields.label: Could you go SOLO for the first 6 months and add them later?

lessons.coaching_moment: If you can't answer 'hard conversation' honestly — you're not ready to be co-founders. That's not bad news. It's a save.

lessons.title: Stayzilla — Homestays, before they were cool
lessons.headline: India's first homestay aggregator. Shut down before Airbnb won India.
lessons.what_they_tried: Built a marketplace of 1 lakh+ homestays across small Indian towns — places hotels didn't reach.
lessons.why_they_failed: Couldn't make unit economics work. Each booking cost more in support than it earned. Investors stopped funding losses.
lessons.lesson_text: First doesn't mean winning. If every order loses money, scale makes it worse, not better.

lessons.title: Doodhwala — Milk delivery, shut by Covid
lessons.headline: Daily milk subscription. Closed before turning a profit.
lessons.what_they_tried: Subscription milk + groceries delivered to your door before 7 AM in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad.
lessons.why_they_failed: Razor-thin margins on milk + heavy subsidies + a parent company that went bankrupt = no runway.
lessons.lesson_text: If the underlying margin is 5 rupees, no amount of growth saves you.

lessons.title: TinyOwl — Food delivery, before Zomato won
lessons.headline: Funded ₹163 cr. Couldn't survive against Swiggy and Zomato.
lessons.what_they_tried: Food ordering app focused on Mumbai, with promised 30-minute delivery.
lessons.why_they_failed: Burned money on driver subsidies and marketing without building real customer love. Co-founders fought publicly.
lessons.lesson_text: If your only difference is 'cheaper or faster,' a richer competitor can copy that in a weekend.

lessons.title: Dazo — Cloud kitchens, too early
lessons.headline: Cooked-meal startup, shut after 2 years.
lessons.what_they_tried: Cooked fresh meals in cloud kitchens, delivered to office workers in Bengaluru.
lessons.why_they_failed: Too far ahead of the market. Customers weren't ready to order lunch on an app, and infrastructure (UPI, delivery fleets) hadn't matured yet.
lessons.lesson_text: Being right but early is the same as being wrong. Time the market, not just the idea.

lessons.title: Askme.com — 4,000 employees, shut overnight
lessons.headline: Local search + commerce platform. Closed when investor pulled out.
lessons.what_they_tried: Just-Dial-style local search + e-commerce + grocery + payments — all at once.
lessons.why_they_failed: Did too many things, none excellently. One investor (Astro Malaysia) controlled funding; when they exited, 4,000 people lost their jobs.
lessons.lesson_text: Don't put all your funding in one investor's hands. And do one thing world-class before doing a second.

lessons.title: Housing.com — Dazzling tech, founder drama
lessons.headline: Built India's best real-estate map. Lost it to leadership chaos.
lessons.what_they_tried: Used aerial imagery, data, and beautiful design to fix Indian real-estate listings.
lessons.why_they_failed: The young CEO publicly attacked investors. Board kicked him out. Product stalled while leadership rebuilt.
lessons.lesson_text: How you treat your team and investors matters as much as your product.

lessons.title: Failing Is Part of the Journey

content.intro: Every founder you admire failed first. Many times. The difference between a failed entrepreneur and a successful one isn't talent — it's that the successful one kept going one more day.

stories.name: Ritesh Agarwal (OYO)
stories.moment: First app rejected. Pivoted from listing budget hotels to running them.

stories.name: Falguni Nayar (Nykaa)
stories.moment: Started Nykaa at 50, after a corporate career ended. Built India's first beauty unicorn.

stories.name: Bhavish Aggarwal (Ola)
stories.moment: First customer cancelled mid-ride and refused to pay. Used the experience to design driver standards.

content.key_takeaway: Every founder's story has more 'no's than 'yes's. The yes's are louder because they came AFTER the no's.
content.mento_says: When something doesn't work, you have two choices: blame yourself, or get curious. Curious always wins.

lessons.coaching_moment: Failure isn't the opposite of success — it's part of the path. The only real failure is stopping.

lessons.title: Reflection: Your Own 'No' Moment

prompts: Tell me about a time you tried something and it didn't work.
Looking back, what would you tell your past self?

lessons.coaching_moment: Writing about a setback turns it from a wound into a lesson. Be honest with yourself.

lessons.title: 🌟 The Complaint Detective — Simulation Challenge
lessons.game_purpose: The full loop: hear a complaint → 5 WHYs → PAIN/SIZE/GAP → customer profile → 60-sec pitch.
lessons.coaching_moment: This is the capstone. Use everything from Weeks 1-3: notice, dig, test, pitch.

lessons.title: Bonus: Startup Founder's Journey
lessons.game_purpose: Run a full startup arc and see how your decisions shape the business.
lessons.coaching_moment: Founder's journey is messy by design. Survive the chaos and you've earned the title.

lessons.title: Worksheet: The Entrepreneur's Pledge

fields.name: my_problem
fields.label: The problem I will keep working on

fields.name: my_helper
fields.label: One person I will ask for help

schema.honor_text: I pledge to be CURIOUS. I will listen to complaints, dig with the Five WHYs, test before I build, and pitch with empathy.

lessons.coaching_moment: Writing your pledge in your own words makes it stick. Read it out loud — that locks it in.

lessons.title: Module Final Quiz
lessons.summary: Last 5 questions before your certificate. You've got this.
lessons.coaching_moment: Whatever you score — you've finished a 4-week journey. That's a real entrepreneurial habit.

fields.question: Failing is…

options.label: Important data on what to do differently

fields.explanation: Every founder fails. The ones who win treat failure as data, not damage.

fields.question: When testing your idea on real customers, you should…

options.label: Tell them what they should think
Ask, listen, watch their reactions, take notes
Tell them only the good parts

fields.explanation: Listening > selling. The customer always knows things you don't.

fields.question: After 4 weeks, the most useful entrepreneurial habit you've learned is probably…
fields.explanation: The mindset of curiosity is the engine. Tools and terms are downstream of that.

fields.question: If a customer says 'Cool but I won't buy that' you should…

options.label: Find another customer who'll say yes

fields.explanation: A NO with reasons is more valuable than a polite YES. Ask why, and pivot if needed.

fields.question: Your Entrepreneur's Pledge is…

options.label: A promise to stay curious, listen, and try

fields.explanation: The pledge is your North Star — curiosity over fear, listening over loudness, action over waiting.

lessons.title: Quest: Pitch out loud
lessons.prompt: Say your 60-second pitch out loud to one real person right now (parent, sibling, friend). Type their reaction in one line.
lessons.completion_message: You just shipped your first pitch.

lessons.title: Byju Raveendran — From village teacher to ed-tech founder
lessons.backstory: Byju was a teacher who made students fall in love with math. He started teaching small batches, then stadiums of 25,000 students, then built an app. BYJU'S became the world's most valuable ed-tech company. (It also struggled later — a reminder that growth alone isn't success.)
lessons.takeaway: Teaching well is a real business skill — and one bad chapter doesn't erase the early ones.
lessons.reflection_prompt: What's something you can teach a younger kid better than their teacher?

lessons.title: Kunal Shah — Failed first, then built CRED
lessons.backstory: Kunal sold FreeCharge (recharge app) to Snapdeal. Then he started CRED — a credit-card rewards app — by noticing one tiny insight: India's most creditworthy people pay bills late on bad apps. CRED only let in users with 750+ credit score.
lessons.takeaway: Niche down. The most valuable users often feel underserved.
lessons.reflection_prompt: Who are the 'best' customers in your idea — and are they being ignored?

lessons.title: Ghazal Alagh — Mamaearth from parent struggles
lessons.backstory: Ghazal couldn't find safe, toxin-free products for her newborn son. She and her husband started making them. Within 7 years, Mamaearth became a publicly listed company with millions of customers.
lessons.takeaway: The best business ideas often come from being a frustrated customer yourself.
lessons.reflection_prompt: What's a product *you* are frustrated with as a kid right now?

lessons.title: Bhavish Aggarwal — Ola from a bad cab ride
lessons.backstory: Bhavish was stranded on a Bangalore-Bandipur trip when a taxi driver abandoned him mid-route. He went home and built Ola — a way to book a cab from your phone with a fair price. Today Ola also builds electric scooters in India.
lessons.takeaway: One bad day can be a billion-rupee idea — if you act on it.
lessons.reflection_prompt: What was the last time *you* were stranded or stuck because of bad service?

lessons.title: Your neighborhood founder
lessons.founder_name: The aunty / uncle on your street
lessons.backstory: Not every founder is on TV. The aunty making tiffins, the uncle running the chai stall, the bhaiya repairing phones — each of them solved a real problem, raised their own capital, hired their first employee, and survived a tough year. They are founders too.
lessons.takeaway: Entrepreneurship doesn't need a hoodie or a Twitter account. It needs a customer and the courage to start.
lessons.reflection_prompt: Pick one neighborhood entrepreneur near you. Ask them one question this week. Write what they said.

lessons.title: Bonus: What is Udyam (and why a tiny business registers)?
lessons.body: Udyam is the Indian government's free, online registration for small businesses. It takes 10 minutes and gives you a unique business ID. Why bother? Banks give you cheaper loans. Government tenders ('orders') become available. Some subsidies open up. You don't need it to start a business — but the moment you're earning, it's worth doing. (This is a general overview, not legal advice.)
lessons.transcript: Udyam is the Indian government's free, online registration for small businesses. It takes 10 minutes...

lessons.title: Bonus: GST in 3 minutes
lessons.body: GST is a single tax that replaced a confusing pile of older taxes in 2017. If your business earns more than ₹20 lakh a year (₹40 lakh for goods in most states), you must register for GST. Below that, you don't. When you do register, you charge customers GST on top of your price — but you can also claim back GST you paid on supplies. (This is a general overview, not legal advice.)
lessons.transcript: GST is a single tax that replaced a confusing pile of older taxes...

lessons.title: Bonus: Why your business needs its OWN bank account
lessons.body: The moment you start charging real customers, open a separate bank account just for your business. Why? You'll actually know if you're making money — personal expenses won't hide in the numbers. Customers trust an account in your business name. And taxes get 10x easier at year-end. Most Indian banks have free 'small business' accounts. Ask. (This is a general overview, not legal advice.)
lessons.transcript: The moment you start charging real customers, open a separate bank account...

lessons.title: Bonus: Money Isn't Dirty (and other lies you'll hear)
lessons.body:
You will meet two voices growing up. One says 'making money is greedy'. Another says 'making money is everything'. Both are wrong, and both will slow you down.

Here's a healthier story: Money is a thank-you note. When a stranger pays you, they're saying 'this saved me time, or pain, or boredom — and it was worth it'. Every rupee a real customer hands you is a vote that you solved a real problem.

Entrepreneurs who hate money build broke companies that close. Entrepreneurs who only love money build slimy companies that get caught. The ones who last treat money as feedback — not as the trophy. The trophy is the problem you fixed. The money tells you you fixed it well.
lessons.transcript: You will meet two voices growing up. One says making money is greedy. Another says making money is everything. Both are wrong. Money is a thank-you note: when a stranger pays you, they're saying you solved a real problem. Entrepreneurs who hate money build broke companies. Entrepreneurs who only love money get caught. The ones who last treat money as feedback, not as the trophy.

lessons.title: Bonus: How to Hear 100 No's Without Quitting
lessons.body:
Every founder you admire has been rejected more times than you. Ritesh Agarwal got rejected by hotels in Delhi for months. Falguni Nayar pitched Nykaa to investors who passed. Rejection is not the bug — it's the road.

Here's the Mento trick: don't take rejection as 'you are bad'. Take it as data. After every 'no', ask exactly two questions:

1. 'What would have made this a yes for you?' — Their answer is the actual lesson.
2. 'Who do you know who'd want this?' — Even a no can give you the next yes.

Set a quota. Aim for 30 no's a month. If you hit 30, the universe will throw in a yes. If you stop at 3 no's, you'll never know the yes was waiting at no number 14.

And remember: a 'no today' is not 'no forever'. Most yeses arrived after the founder followed up six months later — older, sharper, better.
lessons.transcript: Every founder you admire has been rejected more times than you. Rejection is data, not verdict. After every no, ask two questions: 'What would have made this a yes?' and 'Who do you know who'd want this?' Set a quota: aim for 30 no's a month. Most yeses arrive after six months of follow-up. A no today is not no forever.

lessons.title: Bonus: How to Talk to Your Parents About Not Picking a 'Safe' Career
lessons.body:
Your parents love you. That's why they're scared. Indian families spent generations building enough stability that you could even consider being an entrepreneur — and the idea that you'd take a risk with that stability feels reckless to them. It is not selfish to chase your idea. It is also not selfish for them to worry.

Three rules for the hard kitchen-table conversation:

ONE — Don't pitch them. They are not investors. Pitching to parents makes them feel like customers being sold to. Instead, share your homework. Show them the 5 customer interviews from Week 2. Show them the unit economics. Show them the demand test results. Evidence calms fear.

TWO — Frame it as 'AND', not 'OR'. 'I will keep my grades up AND build this on weekends.' 'I will write the entrance exams AND run this as a side business.' Parents say no to OR. They say maybe to AND.

THREE — Give them a milestone, not a forever-promise. 'Give me 6 months. If by then I haven't earned ₹X / signed up Y customers / hit Z, I'll shelve it and focus on college.' A milestone is a deal they can agree to. Forever is a fight.

And one more thing: your parents may surprise you. Most Indian parents secretly admire the kid who actually tries something — they just need to see you've thought it through. Bring the evidence.
lessons.transcript: Your parents love you, so they're scared. Don't pitch them — share your homework. Show your customer interviews, your unit economics, your demand test. Frame it as 'AND' not 'OR' — grades AND this idea. Give a milestone, not a forever-promise: 'Give me 6 months and these targets, or I shelve it.' Parents say no to forever; they say maybe to milestones.

lessons.title: 🎥 Week 4 Live with Mento: Founder's Q&A
lessons.summary: Open Q&A with a working founder (or alum). Bring your hardest unanswered question.
lessons.coaching_moment: Live sessions are where peers catch each other's blind spots. Show up with your worksheet open.

points: Failure isn't the opposite of success — it's part of the path
Sign your founder's pledge — own your journey
